description: What a visitor is asked to download, per project class. Every number here was measured from a real build before it was written down; the headroom column says how much was allowed and why. tooling/lib/payload-budget.mjs is the code that measures and compares, and config/gate-producers.json is what connects the result to the performance convergence gate.
rules: Measured before set. A budget is a recorded baseline plus stated headroom, never a round figure that sounded strict. Raising one is a diff that has to say what earned it.

Per class, because the renderers differ in kind. A static content build ships a document per route and no script; an application build ships one shell and one bundle. One number would be wrong for both.

Only what a class controls. Total bytes and total HTML scale with how many pages a project has, which is the project's property and not the class's, so the byte budgets cover the shared payload and one document at a time.
A class with no entry here is measured and reported and fails nothing. Silence about a class is not a pass, and the report says which it is.
baselineSource: npm run generate:acceptance, then npm install && npm run build in each generated project. The canonical fixtures, not a real business.

marketing-site.headroom: css +25% because the shared stylesheet grows with every section type the composer can emit; document +43% because copy length is the project's. js stays at 0: the static renderer's claim is zero client JavaScript, and an island that needs some is a reviewed change to this line rather than a quiet regression.
marketing-site.floor: minRouteDocuments 2 rather than the measured 4 — page count is the project's, but a static build that emitted one document would be an application shell wearing a static renderer, and that is a class defect.

content-site.headroom: Same shared stylesheet and the same reasoning as marketing-site; a content site is the class most likely to grow long documents, so the per-document budget is deliberately the same generous one.

b2b-saas.headroom: js +13%. The measured 426KB is the framework, router and generated modules before a project adds anything, and it is a finding rather than a comfortable number — recorded here so the next thing that inflates it has to say so. Tightening it is Phase 6 work with a real profile behind it, not a guess today.

consumer-app.headroom: As b2b-saas: the same shell, the same framework, and the same recorded starting point plus 13%.

internal-tool.headroom: As b2b-saas. An internal tool is the class where a large bundle costs least, and it still gets the same ceiling so a regression is visible everywhere it happens.

ai-app.headroom: As b2b-saas: the same application shell and the same recorded starting point. An AI feature's own payload arrives on top of this and is the project's, not the class's.
